Losses due to implementation of VAT 
*623. SHRI GAYA SINGH :† 
           SHRI V V RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the revenue losses suffered by States following 
the implementation of Value Added Tax (VAT) would be compensated by the 
Central Government; and 
(b) if so, the details of the losses estimated to be incurred by each State/UT 
1. the amount compensated by the Central Government ? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) and(b) A 
tement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Keeping in view the request of the States, the Government 
of India has agreed to compensate the revenue loss, if any, upon 
introduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) by the States and Union 
Territories at the rate of 100 per cent in the first year (2003-04), 75 per 
cent in the second year (2004-05) and 50 per cent in the third year 
(2005-06). Assessment of loss, if any, on account of introduction 
of VAT is possible only after its actual implementation by individual 
States/Union Territories. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Gaya Singh.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA : The hon. Minister has mentioned about 
this 100 per cent, 75 per cent and 50 per cent reimbursement, but in the last 
sentence he says, "assessment of loss, if any, on account of introduction of VAT is 
possible only after it is actually implemented." Now, what is the basis on which 
this 100 per cent, 75 per cent and 50 per cent has been calculated, when they do 
not know what is the assessment of loss ? This is a very vague assessment or 
there is no assessment at all. This is a vague decision. And the second point, Sir, 
is this. Why such losses should be incurred by the States at all ? If it is a new 
system, States should still continue to make the same. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH : The hon. Member  suggests that this is a vague 
statement. I think it is very specific. It is 100 per cent, 75 per cent and 50 per 
cent, in the first, second and the third year respectively.

[6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
 
How has it been fixed or arrived at ? In consultation with the States. How will the 
loss be assessed ? The loss cannot be assessed, unless it is actually incurred. It is 
assumed, it is apprehended that there will be a loss in transferring from one 
system to another; that is why, as a surety and a security, the Centre stood in to 
say, "Till you settle down, in the first year we will meet the loss fully; thereafter, a 
little less and little less". It is a perfectly valid system. There is no ambiguity in it. 
SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : Sir, the VAT will be the most important tax 
reform. I would like to ask the hon. Minister through you, Sir, to what extent has there 
been a progress in bringing about uniformity in the legislation, because one of the reasons 
why the VAT is being opposed, is because of some of the draconian provisions in laws 
that are being proposed by States even like Maharashtra. They tend to introduce 
Inspector Raj and such other things. So, is there some progress ? I would also like to 
know whether the Consultative Committee had also raised this issue at its last hearing 
before the Empowered Committee of the State Finance Ministers on this matter in 
particular. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH : Sir, this too has been answered at quite a considerable 
length. The Union Government circulated a model legislation in this regard, which was 
as a guide to the various States, because, essentially, this is a State subject, and it is a 
State law. What some of the States did was to wholesale lift their Sales Tax laws 
along with the penal provision and transfer them to the proposed VAT law. What we 
need as a uniformity across the country is in regard to not only the revenue-neutral rate of 
twelve and-a-half per cent,' but also what are the items under that revenue-neutral rate 
of twelve and-a-half per cent, what is the commodity classification, what are the various 
exemptions, etc. Of course, the States are free to have differentials of penal provision 
they wish to adopt. But it is necessary that, by and large, across the country, the penal 
provisions are more or less the same and, that the apprehensions that -have been 
created in the minds of the various segments of industry, trade, etc. are also put to 
rest. These are some aspects of it.

*626. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI : W ill the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether the debt swap announced in the Budget for 2003-04 requires 
States to forego 20 per cent of their small savings; 
(b) if so, what would be its impact on State finances;

years, State-wise; and

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH) : (a) to (d) 
A Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) For the current year, 30% of the Net Small Savings due to States will be 
used for the debt swap. 
(b) The Scheme envisages that over a three-year period ending in 2004-05, 
all State loans to the Government of India bearing coupons of 13% and above 
would be swapped. Consequently, the States will save an estimated Rs. 81000 
crore in interest and deferred loan repayments, over the residual maturity period 
of the loans. Furthermore, this scheme will restrain the debt build up in States 
through the small savings scheme.

Statement 
(a) to (c) There is no proposal for taking loan by the Government from the

country and policy aspects. The data on water resources used from time to time 
are the current data. There is no proposal under consideration or contemplated 
by the Government of India for privatization of rivers in the country. The National 
Water Policy inter-alia provides for private sector participation in planning, 
development and management of water resources projects for diverse uses 
wherever feasible. Depending upon specific situation, various combination of 
private sector participation for providing water resources facilities may be 
considered.

aimed at fiscal consolidation.

Statement 
Guidelines formulated for issue of licences to photographers for the 
centrally protected monuments at Agra including 
Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri etc. 
 Any photographer who is a citizen of India and not below 18 years of age 
and possesses the requisite skill and expertise to operate a still camera shall 
be eligible to apply for a licence for photography. The applicant for licence 
need not necessarily own a studio. 
 No applicant shall be eligible to submit more than one application. 
 If the applicant for licence is a finn/company/registered society, the 
application should be signed by the person duly authorised to do so by the 
firm/company/registered society as the case may be. 
 The applications received for licences shall be scrutinised by a committee 
headed by the Additional Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, 
who may recommend issuance of licence or otherwise to Director General, 
Archaeological Survey of India, whose decision in this regard shall be final. 
 5Any person selected for issue of licence shall have to pay a non-refundable 
licence fee of Rs.5,000/- (Rupees five thousand only) by way of demand 
draft in favour of the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India to be 
deposited with the Agra Circle, Agra. 
 6 The applicant shall be required to submit alongwith his application proof 
of his age. 
 On receipt of the prescribed licence fee, the Superintending Archaeologist, 
Archaeological Survey of India, Agra Circle, shall issue the requisite licence 
42 

[6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
which shall be for a period of 3 years to the concerned applicant alongwith 
a photo identity card with an appropriate hologram. 
 The licence shall be non transferable. It shall be renewable on payment of a 
licence fee of Rs.5,000/- in the same manner as prescribed for issue of fresh 
licence, if there has been no violation of the terms and conditions of the 
licence and is considered fit for renewal by the Superintending 
Archaeologist, Agra Circle. 
 The licensee will limit his photography  operations to the monument for 
which the licence has been issued. 
 10 The licensee shall display his identity card prominently while 
operating within the precincts of the monuments and shall be dressed neatly 
and will observe etiquette and courtesy at all time to all visitors. He 
should also present his licence for in spection on demand by the officers 
of the Archaeological Survey of India. 
 The issue of licences shall be without prejudice to the rights of the tourists 
and visitors to use their own cameras and take photographs within the 
monuments 
 The licensee shall not charge from th e visitors, a price for photography, 
which is more than that fixed by the Superintending Archaeologist, Agra 
Circle. The licensee shall keep with him a chart of the approved rates duly 
signed by the Superintending Archaeologist, Agra Circle and shall ensure 
that the photographs are de livered to his clients within a reasonable time 
which shall not exceed 5 days. 
 The licensee will give a printed receipt to the clients for the money received 
by him in advance for delivering the photographs at the assigned place. 
 If complaints are received against the licensee, the Superintending 
Archaeologist, Agra Circle, shall issue a warning on the first occasion and a 
second complaint shall result in cancellation of the licence after a summary 
enquiry. 
 In the event of the loss of licence, the licensee shall inform the Superintending 
Archaeologist, Agra Circle, in writing and file an FIR with the police station 
straight away, and a fresh duplicate licence shall be issued on payment of 
Rs.250/-asfee.

IRDA's report on pension reforms 
4688. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state : 
 whether Insurance Regulatory Development Authority (IRDA) 
has submitted a report to Government on pension reforms; 
 if so, what are the recommendations of IRDA in this regard; 
 whether Government have considered the Report and taken a 
decision on the recommendations ; and 
 if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL) : (a) The 
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) has submitted a report 
on Pension Reforms in the "Unorganised Sector" to the Government. 
(b) The main features of the proposed pension system recommended by 
IRDA are:— 
(i) The system is envisaged as a purely voluntary one with both the 
participation and the contributions being voluntary. 
(ii) The system is primarily aimed at  the unorganised sector that is not 
covered by any currently available pension scheme. 
(iii) The system ensures an organi sation which will interface with the 
contributors and the regulator. 
7 6 

[6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) The system shall have an emphasis on low and clear charges to enable 
customers to compare easily the different plans. 
(v) The emphasis on competition through a system of multiple providers 
shall ensure that these strive consistently to out perform each other on costs, 
fund management, and customer service. 
(vi) The system would regulate providers and products as well as the selling 
process thereof, thus reducing cost and complexity while maintaining the security 
of the peoples' funds. 
(vii) The system should also plan for a compulsory annuitisation of a certain 
threshold level; withdrawal or commut ations of the accumulated corpus for 
certain specified reasons would be permitted beyond this amount. 
(c) and (d) The Government has announced in the Budget 2003-04 the 
introduction of a new pension system, which would offer a basket of pension 
policies. The system envisages voluntary participation on defined contribution 
basis which will be portable, allowing transfer of benefits in case of change of 
employment and will go into " individual pension accounts" with pension Fund. 
However, there will be no contribution from the Government in respect of non-
Government employees/individuals. In addition, Government also announced a 
"Varishtha Pension Bima Yojana" through which a pensioner, or any citizen 
above 55 years of age could on payment of a lump-sum amount get benefits 
calculated at 9% per annum. This scheme will be implemented through Life 
Insurance Corporation of India (LIC).

Complaints of credit card holders 
4727. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state : 
 whether a US Consumer Court has ruled that Visa and Master Card 
should refund alteast $500 million for poor disclosure of fees to card holders 
using such cards overseas; 
 if so, whether this ruling will compensate the card holders who have paid 
excess currency conversion fee and surcharge since 1996; 
 whether there have been persistent complaints from credit card holders 
in India about clandestine accounting procedures adopted by credit card 
companies/banks; and 
 if so, what steps are being taken by Government to protect the interest of 
credit card holders? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) Reserve 
Bank of India (RBI) have reported that a US state court case alleged that Master Card's 
method of converting currencies on U.S. issued Master Cards used for the purchase of 
goods or services in a foreign country was an unfair and unlawful business practice. The 
case alleged that Master Card methodology, which the plaintiffs characterize as a "fee" 
grossly exceeded any costs that Master Card incurs in connection with foreign 
currency conversions, and was not properly disclosed to card-holders. The court 
found that the practice is deceptive under state law, and ordered that Master Card 
mandate that members disclose the currency conversion process to card-holders in 
card-holder agreements, applications, solicitations and monthly billing statements. He 
also ordered unspecified restitution to California card-holders. 
More than a dozen federal lawsuits are taking Visa and Master Card to task over 
foreign currency conversion charges. The suits claim the fees charged by Visa, Master 
Card and several major banks for purchases made outside the United States are 
excessive and violate the Truth-in-Lending Act. 
Both Visa and Master Card are technically associations that provide 
transaction services to the banks who actually issue credit cards to their customers. 
The final decision on currency conversions and other fees rests with individual banks. 
(c) and (d) RBI have further reported that credit card is basically a payment facility 
and as credit is incidental, the interest rate directives of RBI on loans and advances do not 
apply to the fees/service charges imposed on credit cards. Credit card dues being in the 
nature of other non-priority sector personal loans, banks are free to determine the rate 
of interest without reference to the Prime Lending Rate. Each bank makes an estimate 
of its costs depending upon the volume, technology adopted, facilities offered etc. for 
fixing the service charges.

Corporate Debt Restructuring 
4732. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 what are the new rules issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on 
Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR); 
 whether the CDR mechanism has been working efficiently; and 
 how many CDR proposals have been finalized since the inception of the 
schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VTTHOB A ADSUL): (a) Based on 
the recommendations of a High Level Group, Reserve Bank of India issued 
revised guidelines on 5th February, 2003. The main features of the revised 
guidelines are the introduction of two types of restructuring under the CDR 
system. Accounts, which are classified as 'standard and sub-standard', would 
be restructured under the first category (Category-I) whereas Accounts classified 
as 'doubtful' would be restructured under the second category (Category-II). 
Guidelines have also been revised in regard to composition and enhancement in 
the scope of Core Group, Additional functions for CDR Empowered Group, 
 121 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2003] 
flexibility in sanction of additional assistance as part of restructuring package, 
introduction of an 'exit option' from the package, restructuring of 'doubtful' assets 
under Category-II guidelines, discretion to institutions like UTT, LIC, GIC, etc. to join 
the CDR on transaction-specific basis. 
According to Reserve Bank of India and CDR Core Group, CDR mechanism is 
working satisfactorily. 
28 proposals have been finalized so far under CDR mechanism since its inception in 
March, 2002 and till 31st March, 2003.

Imbalance of water 
4780. SHRIK. RAMA MOHANA RAO : W ill the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that because of the prohibitive cost and long gestation 
period, river linking project has not yet been cleared; and 
 the steps proposed to re-orient water management policy linking it with 
the poverty alleviation programme to save regional imbalance of water? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) No, Sir. The Ministry of Water 
Resources, then known as the Ministry of Irrigation, formuJated a National Perspective Plan 
for water resources development in 1980 which envisages inter linkages among Peninsular 
Rivers and Himalayan Rivers for transferring water from water surplus basins to water 
deficit areas for optimum utilisation of water resources. Government of India has 
established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) in 1982 
162 

[6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
as an autonomous society to canyout water balance and other studies and prepare 
feasibility reports. NWD A has identified 30 links under the National Perspective for 
preparation of the feasibility reports. The Pre-feasibility Reports of all the links and 
Feasibility Reports of 8 links have been completed. The Central Government has 
constituted a Task Force on Inter-linking of rivers under the Chairmanship of Shri 
Suresh P. Prabhu, Member of Parliament, Lok Sabhaon 13-12-2002. The Task Force 
is working to suggest and guide the task of achieving the goal of inter-linking of 
rivers by the end of 2016 as per its terms of reference. 
(b) There is no proposal under consideration of the Government for re-
orienting existing National Water Policy which however covers water management 
aspects. There is also a provision in the policy for transfer of water from surplus 
areas to deficit areas.

whether the United Nations has lately prepared the first ever World Water

if so, whether India despite its rich river water resources ranks 120th of the 122

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES SHRIMATI BDOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 'United Nations World 
Water Development Report—Water for people, Water for Life', has been released on the 
eve of Third World Water Forum held during March, 2003. 
As per the report, India has been ranked 120th among 122 nations in the world 
in terms of quality of water and 133rd among 180 nations in terms of water 
availability. 
As per the assessment made by the Central Water Commission, the average 
annual water availability in the river systems of the country is assessed at 1869 Billion 
Cubic Meter (BCM). The water resources are assessed river basin-wise. The per capita 
availability of water as per population census figures of the year 2001 is 1820 cubic metre 
per year on a national level. The highest per capita average availability of water in the 
country is estimated as 16,990 cubic metre annually in Minor River Basins Draining into 
Bangladesh and Myanmar followed by 13,636 cubic metre annually in Brahmaputra-
Barak Sub-basin and the lowest per capita average availability of water in the country is 
estimated as 298 cubic metre annually in Sabarmati basin. 
The per capita availability of water, river basin-wise, is given in the one close 
statement (see below). As per the United Nations World Water Development 
Report, Green land has the highest per capita water availability of 10,767,857 cubic

Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins. 
Several steps have been taken for improvement/restoration of quality of 
water bodies in the country and some of them are :

(ii) Issuance of Directives to the defaulting industries for preventing

Prevention of flood in Assam due to Brahamputra River 
4783. SHRI  DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the MINISTER OF 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 the steps proposed to prevent frequent flooding in the State of Assam 
due to Brahamputra River; 
 whether Government are aware of the loss to the farmers and common 
people due to flood in the State during the last two decades; and 
 whether any concrete proposals have been formulated in this regard, if 
so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATIBUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Hood Management being a 
State subject, investigation, planning and implementation of flood management 
schemes are within the purview of the State Government. The Central Government 
renders assistance which are technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. 
Considering the magnitude and complexity of the flood problem in the North 
East, the Government of India has set up Brahmaputra Board under an Act of Parliament 
i.e. Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980 (46 of 1980). The Board has prepared the Master 
Plans for the control of floods and bank erosion and improvement of drainage in the 
Brahmaputra and Barak Valley also given due regards to the development and 
utilisation the water resources for irrigation, hydropower, navigation and other 
beneficial use. These Master Plans which suggest various short term and long term

Water scarcity 
4786. DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY : 
SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL :  
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 whether the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisations has 
pointed out that although there was no global water crisis, there were serious 
water and food security problems in some developing countries; 
 if so, whether in the rep irt, India also has been considered as one of 
the scarcity threat of water nation; 
 if so, the main reasons mentioned in the report; 
 the other countries where shortage of water will continue; and 
 what steps are being taken to meet the water scarcity in the coming 
years? 
THE MINISTER OF STAIE IN THE MINISTRY OF WAIER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) As per the Report entitled "Unlocking the water potential of 
agriculture", individual countries have not been named as water scarcity nations. 
It indicates that one in five developing countries would face water shortage by 
2030. It is mentioned in the report that irrigated areas in the developing countries 
are expected to increase from currently 205 million hectare to 242 million hectare 
and water withdrawals for irrigation is projected to increase by 14 per cent by 
2030. By 2030, East Asia, the Near East and North Africa would be using three-
quarters of their irrigable land and South Asia almost 90 per cent. 
(e) In order to augment the availability of water in the country for irrigation 
and other uses and for their efficient us e, a large number of dams have been 
constructed thereby creating 177 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) of storage capacity. 
Another 75 BCM of storage will be created on completion of dams which are under 
various stages of construction. Proposals to take up additional dams to create a live 
storage capacity of 132 BCM are also under formulation/considerauon. To accelerate 
creation of irrigation potential by early completion of ongoing schemes, Government 
of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP). Government 
of India is also promoting rainwater harvesting through Watershed Management 
Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and roof-top rainwater harvesting 
under the sector reform project of Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme of the 
Ministry of Rural Development, for which technical and financial assistance is provided 
to the State Governments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water 
170 

(6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Board has also taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground 
Water" on pilot basis. Assistance is also being extended to State Governments 
under Command Area Development (CAD) programme for bridging the gap between 
potential created and utilized. For meeting future requirements of water, as a long 
term measure, National Water Development Agency have formulated National 
Perspective Plan for water resources development which envisages interlinking 
various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from surplus 
basins to water deficit basins.

†4787. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA : Will the Minister of WATER

 whether it is a fact that many harmful chemicals such as arsenic, zinc 
etc. have been found in water in various parts of the country;

other fatal diseases; and 
 if so, the action being taken by Government for treatment of water in

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) : (a) As per studies carried out by the 
Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), under the Ministry of Water Resources, 
ground water in major parts of the country is by and large potable. However, 
ground water has been found contaminated in some parts of the country. The 
names of States and locations where ground water has been found contaminated 
and reasons thereof are given in enclosed Statement (See below). 
(b) and (c) People in parts of West Bengal are suffering from arsenic 
dermotesis and other related problems. Provision of drinking water supply is 
the responsibility of the State Governments. The Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking 
Water Mission has been assisting and guiding the States in provisioning of safe 
drinking water to rural areas under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme 
and exclusive Sub-Mission programmes in areas having serious ground water 
quality problems like fluoride, iron, arsenic and brackishness. In such areas 
where ground water is unfit for drinking, safe drinking water is provided through 
alternative sources, either by tapping surface water or by undertaking remedial 
measures like de-fluoridation, iron and arsenic removal.

4791. SHRI R P.GOENKA:Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state : 
 whether it is a fact that France has recently offered to extend its expertise 
and technologies to India in the fiel d of water, waste and environment 
management; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether it is also a fact that similar expertise has been extended by 
France in related disciplines for four other research projects already in progress 
in Chennai and other research centres; and 
 if so, the details thereof, including an evaluation of the projects being 
implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a)and(b) Yes, Sir. The 
French Government has shown interest to provide assistance to some projects 
for cooperation with Indian Academic and Scientific Institutions through counter-
part agencies in Water Management Sector. An Indo-French Working Group 
has been constituted on Urban Development in the Ministry of Urban 
Development and Poverty Alleviation for exchange of information between the 
officials of the two countries and to promote bilateral cooperation in the areas of 
(i) Waste Management; (ii) Water Management; (iii) Infrastructure Development; 
(iv) Natural Disaster Mitigation; and (v) Urban Transport. The first meeting of 
the Working Group was held on 24th-25th April, 2003. Presently, two projects 
namely, (i) Sewage Infrastructures for city of Imphal and (ii) Digital Mapping 
Information System for Bangalore Metropolitan area at an estimated cost of 
Euro 8.735 and 4.560 million respectively are under implementation in the country. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. An Indo-French Unit for Water and Waste Technologies 
has been established at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi on 27-2-2002 for 
which an Agreement was reached with French side on 9-3-2000. This facility 
shall be used to train field engineers working in Government industries and the 
NGOs as well as to train University teachers and facilitate advanced technology 
transfer in the field of water and waste. 
Under the framework of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed 
between the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore and Institute of Research

Contaminated ground water in Delhi 
4795. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased 
to state: 
whether it is a fact that a joint study conducted by the Central Ground Water Board 
and the Central Pollution Control Board has brought out that Demi's ground water contains 
excessive salinity, nitrate and flourosis, causing extensive damage to the health of the 
inhabitants of the city; and 
if so, the details of short term/long term steps taken to identify the basic causes of the 
contamination and to ensure supply of clean drinking water to the capital? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) A study on the "Status of Ground Water 
Quality and Pollution Aspects in NCT of Delhi" was undertaken jointly by the Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB) and the Central Pollution Control Board during 1997-98. 
The study indicated that ground water quality in some parts of Delhi has higher 
concentration of total dissolved solids, electrical conductivity, chloride, nitrate, 
sulphate and fluoride. 
(b) The short term/long term steps taken to identify the basic causes of 
contamination and to ensure supply of clean drinking water to the capital are as 
follows:— 
(i) CGWB regularly carries out studies on ground water quality in NCT of Delhi. 
During the course of studies, the problematic areas are identified and further 
detailed studies are taken up in such areas. 
(ii) CGWB is monitoring ground water quality in NCT of Delhi on regular basis. 
(iii) CGWB has deployed mobile chemical laboratory in different localities of NCT 
of Delhi and surrounding areas for the benefit of public and to get ground 
water samples analysed. 
(iv) The Delhi Jal Board has identified hand pumps and other structures in the 
polluted areas where the shallow ground water is not fit for human 
consumption and painted them red with warning. 
192 

[6 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Registration of ground water extracting tubewells/boreholes in NCT of 
Delhi by Central Ground Water Authority (CG WA) for streamlining the 
ground water extraction activities. 
(vi) CGWA has notified South and South-West districts of NCT of Delhi 
based on the studies carried out by the CGWB. 
(vii) CGWA has carried out mass awareness campaign to create awareness 
among general public, industrialist and industrial workers regarding 
pollution and over-exploitation of ground water. 
(viii) Pilot projects of rain water harvesting has been taken up in NCT of 
Delhi. 
fix) CGWB has provided technical guidance and assistance to various 
institutions, private agencies, NGO and general public desirous for 
taking up rain water harvesting in their premises. 
Flood prone areas 
47%. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRTYA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
the State-wise flood prone areas in the country recorded in each plan 
period from First to Ninth Five Year Plan; 
whether dams on the rivers are causing dryness/silting of all river beds 
thereby causing floods; and 
if so, the remedial steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Rashtriya Barh Ayog (RBA) has 
assessed the flood prone area in the country as 40 mha. in 1980 using the data on 
flood affected area during 1953—78. 
The flood affected area is collected and reported by Revenue Authorities of 
States. Central Water Commission has compiled the data since 1953 on the basis 
of information received from State Revenue Authorities. The Statement of State-
wise and Plan-wise total flood affected area from 1st Plan to DCth Plan is enclosed 
(See below). 
(b) and (c) Dams do have some morphological impact on the upstream as 
well as downstream of the river. The impact varies from location to location and 
also temporarily. But the hypothesis that dams can cause dryness or silting is 
unfounded in the absence of any back-up scientific study.

this regard. Madam, a time may come when the interest rate may become 
negative. The inflation rate is more than the net interest rate. The  net interest 
rate is three and a half per cent to five, per cent and the inflation rate is six 
per cent to six and a half per cent. This  is a very alarming situation. . The 
Government must be careful about it. The Government has to be careful 
about the investment arising out of the Public Provident Fund. I am told that 
hundreds of crores of rupees of the Public Provident Fund have been 
invested, which are in danger, which are in jeopardy, which may not come 
back. One such example is, the Governme nt invested Rs. 1500 crores in the 
IFCI bonds. For the last two years, they are not paying the interest. The 
Government must look into it. Yesterday, there was a news item that the 
Government was planning to allow the Provident Fund proceeds to be 
invested in equities abroad. I would like to warn the Government not to go 
ahead with such ventures  because they do not ha ve the knowledge as to 
where they should invest abroad and in which scrip. They have failed 
miserably to look after the interests of the people in this country. How will 
they be able to look after the interests of the people by investing abroad? 
Madam, the investment guidelines in regard to PSUs and the Provident Fund 
need to be updated and revised. There are several public sector companies 
which have invested a large amount of money in various companies. MTNL 
is one such example. Shri Sanjay Nirupam also knows it. Suddenly, Rs. 250 
crores were invested in a Government-guaranteed corporation in 
Maharashtra. This money will never come back. Madam, Rs. 250 crores will 
never come back. The Government gave Rs. 250 crores in one shot. 
I support the reduction in the inte rest rate because the industry 
which was borrowing money at a very high rate of interest will now be able 
to compete. Government's debt servicing charges will go down, which will 
be quite helpful. But the rate of interest should not go down so much because 
the pensioners, the old people who are entirely dependent on the proceeds of 
interest, would suffer. 
The Government has a new scheme for guaranteeing 9 per cent 
return through the LIC, for which, I understand, only Rs. 30 crores have been 
provided, which is not enough.

its energies towards creating a peaceful  and economically-p rosperous India. 
Thank you, Madam.

become a developed nation. I hope, this point will be taken care of while

Sir, now I come to some of the exigencies. There are some 
historical necessities. India is a Union of States. At the time of 
Independence, many of the States were very poor, underdeveloped. There 
were also social necessities, and for that, some specific priorities were given,

Sir, I want to draw the attention of the House and also of the 
Finance Ministry to the Special Industrial Policy which was formulated for 
the North Eastern Region in order to give additional incentives so that there is 
employment generation through investment from outside. For that, some 
specific exemptions and some incentives were provided. Sir, it is sad state of 
affairs that after a lapse of four-f ive years, whatever  incentives were 
provided, are gradually, year after year , withdrawn by the Finance Ministry. 
Here, I would like to give two or three examples which would explain what 
has happened and what has been done for the North Eastern Region. These 
are some mere declarations through wh ich some packages are given, but in 
actual effect, this is not given effect to. On December 24, 1997, the Industrial 
Policy for the North Eastern Region was announced, after the Cabinet 
approval, through which tax-holiday for ten years for all the industrial 
activities in the North East was given. On July 8, 1999, in pursuant to the 
Industrial Policy above, exemption in Central Excise for ten years effected 
on all industrial activities in Assam and Tripura. On December 31, 1999, the 
Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue had withdrawn exemption of 
Central Excise in respect of pan masala containing tobacco, tobacco 
products and cigarettes. On January 17, 2000, the Ministry of Finance, 
Department of Revenue, restored the exemption in respect of pan
